newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk Cypriot leader sombre ahead of U.N. talks.
newsitem.headline: Turk Cypriot leader sombre ahead of U.N. talks.

text.p: Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, enroute to a meeting with his Greek Cypriot counterpart, said on Sunday a first round of talks had failed to advance the cause of peace between the rival communities.

"No forward steps were taken on the political scene, and (we can say) it has even gone backwards," Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency quoted Denktash as saying during a stopover in Istanbul before talks on Monday in Switzerland.

Denktash blamed Greek Cypriot President Clafcos Clerides for blocking a proposed exchange of assets between Greek and Turkish Cypriots, saying this doomed international efforts to create bi-zonal federation on the divided island, the agency said.
He also repeated earlier demands that the Greek Cypriots freeze membership talks with the European Union and shelve planned deployment of a Russian-made missile system, set for next summer.
"I think, this meeting will be the last one. If no clarity is reached on the topics mentioned above...(the fact) that we can go nowhere will come to light," Denktash said.
Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been forcibly separated since 1974 when Turkish forces invaded the north in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.

The resulting divison of what was a patchwork of villages into a Turkish north and a Greek south has cut off many on each side from their homes and other property. Restitution remains one of the thorniest issues between the two sides.
The latest talks are set to resume on Monday in Montreux, Switzerland. The two leaders met for a first round last month in Troutbeck, New York.
On the table is a U.N.-drafted document calling on the two communities to commit themselves to a sustained process of open-ended, direct negotiations.

Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence that resulted in the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force that remains on the island.
The Turkish Cypriots proclaimed their own state in 1983 with Denktash as president, but it is recognised only by Ankara.
